article.title: The beep is the second-most-used page of your business: a voicemail greeting script that keeps the caller
article.body_markdown:
Six out of ten calls to small businesses that don't connect end at the beep - and whether the caller stays for the beep or hits redial on the next listing is decided by about four seconds of recorded voice. The voicemail greeting is the second-most-used page of your business and the one nobody ever wrote on purpose. A caller reaching a mailbox is doing maths: will anyone hear this? how long until they call back? is there a faster way? A generic greeting answers none of the three, so the maths comes back unfavourable and the caller moves on.

The script that keeps them - ten minutes to record, once:

- **Line 1, name and promise** - "You've reached Northside Plumbing." Say the business name like you're glad they called.
- **Line 2, the back time** - "we check this box every hour, someone will call you back before 2 pm today." "As soon as possible" is an estimate; "before 2 pm" is a promise, and promises get callbacks.
- **Line 3, what to leave** - name, number, and the one thing you need done; naming the three things callers actually need turns a rambling message into a workable ticket.
- **Line 4, the faster path** - "text this number, or book at northside.com/book - both go straight to the same phone." The text path and booking link convert better than callbacks.
- **Line 5, the urgent path** - "press zero now for the on-call plumber." The difference between "they'll get back to me" and "they're dealing with me now."

Plus: the four variations every mailbox needs (workday, closed, busy, holiday - one greeting is a leak on three days out of four), the recording craft that makes a cheap microphone sound trustworthy (one take standing up, smile on line one, numbers slowly, re-record when anything changes), the test call from a phone that isn't yours, the four traps (the full mailbox - the most expensive sentence in small business; the comedy greeting; the rebrand nobody re-recorded; the mailbox nobody checks), the four-minute monthly audit, and the worked example: a two-chair barbershop whose carrier-default greeting was quietly handing every hung-up call to the shop next door, fixed in one coffee break.

The full script, variations, and audit: [Voicemail Greeting Script - HIVE80lab Ops Notes](https://hive80-lab.github.io/ops-notes/voicemail-greeting-script.html)
